```{r setup}
library(satrct)
```

## Setting

When a randomized controlled trial (RCT) would be underpowered, a single-arm
trial (SAT) is often considered instead. Both designs enrol the same number
$n$ of patients in the current trial. The RCT allocates them to the
experimental treatment and a concurrent control. The SAT gives all $n$
patients the experimental treatment and compares them with an external
control group of $n_E$ patients, or with a fixed threshold ($n_E = \infty$).
The SAT comparison may be biased: its estimate has expectation
$\delta + b$, where $\delta$ is the true effect and $b$ the bias. The package
uses normal approximations with a standard deviation $\sigma$ per patient on
the scale of the treatment effect; `endpoint_sd()` gives $\sigma$ for binary
and time-to-event endpoints.

## Mean squared error and the break-even bias

With 1:1 allocation the RCT estimate has variance $4 \sigma^2 / n$, and the
SAT estimate has mean squared error $\sigma^2 (1 / n + 1 / n_E) + b^2$. The
two are equal at the break-even bias
$b^* = \sigma \sqrt{3 / n - 1 / n_E}$. This condition was given in
random-effects form by Collignon et al. (2020) and follows from Pocock
(1976). The tolerable bias shrinks with the size of the trial:

```{r}
n <- c(20, 40, 80, 160)
data.frame(n = n, b_star = breakeven_bias(n, n_e = 200))
```

With $n = 20$ the SAT has the smaller mean squared error for any bias below
`r round(breakeven_bias(20, n_e = 200), 2)` standard deviations, but with
$n = 160$ the limit is `r round(breakeven_bias(160, n_e = 200), 2)`. For a
given bias, `breakeven_n()` returns the sample size above which the RCT is
preferable:

```{r}
breakeven_n(bias = 0.2, n_e = 200)
```

## A single-arm test with a bias margin

A SAT can be tested with a prespecified bias margin $m$: it rejects when the
estimate exceeds $m$ by more than $z_{1 - \alpha}$ standard errors. Its type
I error is at most $\alpha$ for every bias up to $m$, and grows beyond it.

```{r}
power_sat(n = 40, delta = 0, n_e = 120, bias = c(0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3), margin = 0.2)
```

At zero bias, the SAT with margin $m$ has more power than the RCT when $m$ is
below the critical margin
$\delta (1 - \sqrt{1 + n / n_E} / 2)$:

```{r}
m_c <- critical_margin(n = 40, delta = 0.6, n_e = 120)
m_c
c(rct = power_rct(n = 40, delta = 0.6),
  sat = power_sat(n = 40, delta = 0.6, n_e = 120, margin = m_c))
```

## The matched significance level

Some guidance for small populations considers testing an RCT at a relaxed
significance level. `matched_alpha()` returns the level $\alpha'$ at which
the RCT has the same power as the SAT with margin $m$, and the bias at which
the SAT type I error reaches $\alpha'$:

```{r}
res <- matched_alpha(n = 40, delta = 0.6, n_e = 120, margin = 0.1)
res
```

The RCT tested at the one-sided level
`r signif(res[["alpha_matched"]], 2)` has the power of the SAT without bias
(`r signif(res[["power"]], 2)`). The SAT has the smaller type I error only
while the bias is below `r signif(res[["bias_crossing"]], 2)`, which equals the
critical margin `r signif(critical_margin(40, 0.6, 120), 2)` whatever the
margin.

The comparison matches the RCT to the planned power of the SAT without bias
and then lets the bias vary. A positive bias raises both the type I error and
the power of the SAT, so above the critical margin the SAT is not a worse test
in every respect. If the RCT were instead matched to the power that the SAT has
at the same bias, the SAT would have the smaller type I error at every bias.
The critical margin therefore answers one question: how large the bias may be
before the SAT has a larger risk of a false positive conclusion than an RCT
relaxed to its planned power. Whether the SAT is preferable also depends on
what is assumed about the bias, on the error criterion, on the planned effect
and on the clinical requirements for an external control, which these
calculations do not cover. The calculations use a normal model with known
variances, in which the crossing at the critical margin is exact; for binary
and time-to-event endpoints it is an approximation.

## A random bias and fixed margins

When the bias varies between trials, it can be described by a normal
distribution with mean $\bar{b}$ and standard deviation $\tau$, estimated
for example from benchmarking studies. Two margins can be derived from it
before the trial: $m_{avg}$ keeps the type I error averaged over this
distribution at $\alpha$, and $m_{0.95} = \bar{b} + z_{0.95} \tau$ keeps the
type I error given the bias at most $\alpha$ in 95% of trials.

```{r}
n <- 60
n_e <- 120
delta <- 0.5
b_bar <- 0.1
tau <- 0.1
v_s <- mse_sat(n, n_e)
m_avg <- b_bar + qnorm(0.975) * (sqrt(v_s + tau^2) - sqrt(v_s))
m_95 <- b_bar + qnorm(0.95) * tau
c(m_avg = m_avg, m_95 = m_95, m_crit = critical_margin(n, delta, n_e))
```

The power of the SAT with such a margin can be evaluated without bias or
averaged over the distribution of the bias, and the two differ:

```{r}
sapply(c(m_avg = m_avg, m_95 = m_95), function(m) {
  c(type1_averaged = power_sat(n, 0, n_e, bias = b_bar, margin = m, tau = tau),
    power_without_bias = power_sat(n, delta, n_e, margin = m),
    power_averaged = power_sat(n, delta, n_e, bias = b_bar, margin = m, tau = tau))
})
power_rct(n, delta)
```

With $m_{avg}$, the averaged power exceeds the power of the RCT exactly when
$\tau$ is below the break-even bias, here
`r round(breakeven_bias(60, n_e = 120), 3)`. The margin $m_{0.95}$ exceeds the
critical margin, so the SAT with it is less powerful than the RCT when the
external control is unbiased.

A margin stated in a protocol stays fixed, while the distribution from which
it was derived may be wrong. With $m_{avg}$ kept at `r round(m_avg, 3)`, the
averaged type I error rises when the actual mean or standard deviation of the
bias is larger than planned:

```{r}
c(planned = power_sat(n, 0, n_e, bias = b_bar, margin = m_avg, tau = tau),
  mean_0.2 = power_sat(n, 0, n_e, bias = 0.2, margin = m_avg, tau = tau),
  tau_0.2 = power_sat(n, 0, n_e, bias = b_bar, margin = m_avg, tau = 0.2))
```

These are plug-in calculations at chosen values of $\bar{b}$ and $\tau$. When
the distribution of the bias is estimated from a few studies, a margin can
instead be calibrated on the posterior predictive distribution of the bias of
a new trial, which also reflects the uncertainty of the estimates.

## Sample sizes

`n_rct()` and `n_sat()` return continuous planning values. A trial needs whole
numbers of patients in each group, so the values are rounded up to a feasible
allocation, for example an even total for 1:1 randomization:

```{r}
n_plan <- n_rct(delta = 0.5, power = 0.8)
c(planning_value = n_plan, total = 2 * ceiling(n_plan / 2))
```

## Hybrid designs

Pocock (1976) combined concurrent and external controls. `optimal_nc()`
returns the number of concurrent controls that minimizes the mean squared
error when the bias has prior variance $b^2 + \tau^2$:

```{r}
optimal_nc(n = 200, n_e = 88, tau = c(0.05, 0.1))
```

These are the values 63.9 and 77 of Pocock's Example 2. The SAT is optimal
among hybrid designs when $b^2 + \tau^2 \le \sigma^2 (1 / n - 1 / n_E)$.

## Exact calculations for binary endpoints

For small trials with a binary endpoint, `oc_sat_binary_exact()` gives the
exact binomial test against a threshold, and `oc_binary_exact()` the exact
rejection probability of two-group comparisons, including a SAT compared
with an external control:

```{r}
oc_sat_binary_exact(n = 30, p_t = c(0.3, 0.5), p0 = 0.3, margin = 0.05)
oc_binary_exact(n_t = 30, n_c = 60, p_t = c(0.35, 0.55), p_c = 0.3, margin = 0.05)
```

## References

Collignon O, Schritz A, Senn SJ, Spezia R. Clustered allocation as a way of
understanding historical controls: components of variation and regulatory
considerations. *Statistical Methods in Medical Research* 2020; 29:
1960--1971.

Pocock SJ. The combination of randomized and historical controls in clinical
trials. *Journal of Chronic Diseases* 1976; 29: 175--188.
